claims.source: Although 7-days of single whisker experience is insufficient to produce experience-dependent potentiation in WT barrel cortex (Glazewski and Fox, 1996), three measures indicated faster potentiation in Ccr5+/- mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Glazewski and Fox, 1996).

claims.claim: Penetrations in barrels surrounding D1 revealed potentiated responses to D1 stimulation in Ccr5+/- but not WT mice after 7 days of single whisker experience.
claims.source: First, penetrations in barrels surrounding D1 revealed potentiated responses to D1 stimulation in Ccr5+/- but not WT mice (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data showing potentiated responses in Ccr5+/- mice but not WT mice.

claims.claim: A comparison of each cell's response to the spared versus deprived principal whisker response showed plasticity in Ccr5+/- mice but not in WT mice after 7 days of single whisker experience.
claims.source: Second, a comparison of each cell's response to the spared versus deprived principal whisker response (vibrissae dominance) showed plasticity in Ccr5+/- (Figure 5C, deprived versus undeprived t(21) = 3.222 p<0.01, Student's t-test) but not in WT mice (Figure 5B, deprived versus undeprived, t(11) = 1.663, p>0.05).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of vibrissae dominance data comparing deprived and undeprived conditions in Ccr5+/- and WT mice.

claims.claim: A plot of D1 response versus principal whisker response showed points above the identity line only for Ccr5+/- but not WT mice after 7 days of single whisker experience.
claims.source: Third, a plot of D1 response versus principal whisker (PW) response showed points above the identity line (D1>PW) only for Ccr5+/- but not WT mice (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by graphical representation of electrophysiology data showing the relationship between D1 and PW responses.

claims.claim: Ccr5+/- mice showed a significant increase in weighted vibrissae dominance index (WVDI) after 7 days deprivation compared to WT mice.
claims.source: Comparison of the time course of vibrissae dominance also showed a significant increase in WVDI in Ccr5+/- mice (0.396 ± 0.051), but not in WT mice (0.111 ± 0.011) after 7 days deprivation [Figure 5E; Interaction: F(2,41) = 1.398, genotype, F(1,41) = 8.919, days deprived F(2,41) = 10.20, genotype and deprivation period are significant: t = 3.05, p<0.05, Bonferroni post-tests].
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA with Bonferroni post-tests, p<0.05) of WVDI data comparing Ccr5+/- and WT mice.

claims.claim: Ccr5+/- mice show faster plasticity in the barrel cortex.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that Ccr5+/- mice show faster plasticity in the barrel cortex.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined electrophysiology data showing enhanced experience-dependent plasticity in Ccr5+/- mice.

claims.claim: A spike-timing dependent protocol induced LTP in 20% of L2/3 cells in WT mice.
claims.source: In WT mice, L2/3 cells showed significant LTP in just 20% of cases while in Ccr5+/- and Ccr5-/- mice the same protocol produced LTP in 70% of cases (Figure 6B, χ2 = 15.63, p<0.001, χ-squared test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (χ-squared test, p<0.001) of in vitro electrophysiology data showing the proportion of cells exhibiting LTP.

claims.claim: The same spike-timing dependent protocol produced LTP in 70% of L2/3 cells in Ccr5+/- and Ccr5-/- mice.
claims.source: In WT mice, L2/3 cells showed significant LTP in just 20% of cases while in Ccr5+/- and Ccr5-/- mice the same protocol produced LTP in 70% of cases (Figure 6B, χ2 = 15.63, p<0.001, χ-squared test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (χ-squared test, p<0.001) of in vitro electrophysiology data showing the proportion of cells exhibiting LTP.

claims.claim: WT mice did not show LTP on average with the spike-timing dependent protocol.
claims.source: On average, the WT mice did not show LTP, while the Ccr5+/- and Ccr5-/- mice showed 188.1 ± 1.45% and 164.5 ± 22.5% potentiation, respectively (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro electrophysiology data showing the average magnitude of LTP in WT mice.

claims.claim: Ccr5+/- mice showed 188.1 ± 1.45% potentiation with the spike-timing dependent protocol.
claims.source: On average, the WT mice did not show LTP, while the Ccr5+/- and Ccr5-/- mice showed 188.1 ± 1.45% and 164.5 ± 22.5% potentiation, respectively (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro electrophysiology data showing the average magnitude of LTP in Ccr5+/- mice.

claims.claim: Ccr5-/- mice showed 164.5 ± 22.5% potentiation with the spike-timing dependent protocol.
claims.source: On average, the WT mice did not show LTP, while the Ccr5+/- and Ccr5-/- mice showed 188.1 ± 1.45% and 164.5 ± 22.5% potentiation, respectively (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro electrophysiology data showing the average magnitude of LTP in Ccr5-/- mice.

claims.claim: An increase in ocular dominance plasticity, as well as in learning and memory, is accompanied by a lower synaptic release probability in the cortex in HRasG12V mice.
claims.source: Previous studies with HRasG12V mice suggest that an increase in ocular dominance plasticity, as well as in learning and memory, is accompanied by a lower synaptic release probability in the cortex (Kaneko et al., 2010; Kushner et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kaneko et al., 2010; Kushner et al., 2005).

claims.claim: The release probability was significantly lower in Ccr5+/- and Ccr5-/- mice compared to WT mice in the barrel cortex.
claims.source: The release probability was significantly lower in Ccr5+/- and Ccr5-/- mice (Figure 7B, p<0.01, Kruskal-Wallis test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis test, p<0.01) of in vitro electrophysiology data measuring release probability.

claims.claim: mEPSPs in L2/3 cells of Ccr5+/- mice were smaller compared to WT mice.
claims.source: Consistent with this finding, mEPSPs (Figure 7C) in L2/3 cells of Ccr5+/- mice were smaller (Figure 7D, D(52) = 0.6154 p<0.001, K-S test) and occurred at a lower frequency compared to WT mice (Figure 7E, D(21) = 0.9524 p<0.001, K-S test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (K-S test, p<0.001) of in vitro electrophysiology data measuring mEPSP amplitude.

claims.claim: mEPSPs in L2/3 cells of Ccr5+/- mice occurred at a lower frequency compared to WT mice.
claims.source: Consistent with this finding, mEPSPs (Figure 7C) in L2/3 cells of Ccr5+/- mice were smaller (Figure 7D, D(52) = 0.6154 p<0.001, K-S test) and occurred at a lower frequency compared to WT mice (Figure 7E, D(21) = 0.9524 p<0.001, K-S test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (K-S test, p<0.001) of in vitro electrophysiology data measuring mEPSP frequency.

claims.claim: Lower release probability and smaller, less frequent mEPSPs could create greater 'headroom' for LTP and experience-dependent potentiation in Ccr5 knockout mice.
claims.source: Both effects could create greater 'headroom' for LTP and experience-dependent potentiation in Ccr5 knockout mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed changes in release probability and mEPSPs in Ccr5 knockout mice and their potential impact on plasticity.

claims.claim: The virus exclusively infected neurons in the barrel cortex.
claims.source: Immuno-histochemistry confirmed that the virus exclusively infected neurons (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1, 35% infection rate and 100% co-localization of NeuN and GFP).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing co-localization of GFP with NeuN in the barrel cortex.

claims.claim: Only shRNA-CCR5 mice, but not shRNA-Cont mice, exhibited a shifted vibrissae dominance histogram after 7 days of single whisker experience.
claims.source: Only shRNA-CCR5 mice, but not shRNA-Cont mice, exhibited a shifted vibrissae dominance histogram after 7 days of single whisker experience (Figure 8B, t(10) = 6.485 p<0.001, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.001) of in vivo electrophysiology data comparing vibrissae dominance in mice injected with shRNA-CCR5 vs. shRNA-Cont AAV in the barrel cortex.

claims.claim: Knockdown of Ccr5 in the adult barrel cortex resulted in an experience-dependent plasticity phenotype that closely mirrored that of the Ccr5+/- mice.
claims.source: Knockdown of Ccr5 in the adult barrel cortex resulted in an experience-dependent plasticity phenotype that closely mirrored that of the Ccr5+/- mice (Figure 8C, Ccr5+/- mice t(20) = 2.939 p<0.01, Student's t-test; viral knockdown: t(10) = 6.485 p<0.001, Student's t-test), demonstrating that CCR5 is a suppressor of neocortical plasticity acting directly on neurons in the adult brain.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of in vivo electrophysiology data comparing the plasticity phenotype of Ccr5+/- mice and mice with viral Ccr5 knockdown in the barrel cortex.

claims.claim: CCR5 is a suppressor of neocortical plasticity acting directly on neurons in the adult brain.
claims.source: Knockdown of Ccr5 in the adult barrel cortex resulted in an experience-dependent plasticity phenotype that closely mirrored that of the Ccr5+/- mice (Figure 8C, Ccr5+/- mice t(20) = 2.939 p<0.01, Student's t-test; viral knockdown: t(10) = 6.485 p<0.001, Student's t-test), demonstrating that CCR5 is a suppressor of neocortical plasticity acting directly on neurons in the adult brain.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined results from viral knockdown experiments in adult barrel cortex showing enhanced plasticity when Ccr5 is knocked down in neurons.

claims.claim: The HIV gp120 V3 loop peptide contains the gp120 domain that binds to and activates CCR5.
claims.source: The HIV gp120 V3 loop peptide contains the gp120 domain that binds to and activates CCR5 (Cormier and Dragic, 2002; Galanakis et al., 2009; Morikis et al., 2007; Sirois et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Cormier and Dragic, 2002; Galanakis et al., 2009; Morikis et al., 2007; Sirois et al., 2005).

claims.claim: V3 peptide binds to mouse hippocampal CCR5.
claims.source: Immunoprecipitation with anti-HA-agarose, to co-precipitate V3-HA peptide and CCR5 in mouse hippocampal lysates, demonstrated that V3 peptide binds to mouse hippocampal CCR5 (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing co-precipitation of V3-HA peptide and CCR5 in mouse hippocampal lysates.

claims.claim: V3 treatment completely abolished any instance of LTP and produced an average depression of 27.8% in cells from WT mice in the barrel cortex.
claims.source: In cells from WT mice, V3 treatment had a strong effect on the magnitude and probability of LTP (Figure 9A,B), completely abolishing any instance of LTP and producing an average depression of 27.8% (t(120) = 26.6, p<0.001, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.001) of in vitro electrophysiology data comparing LTP in WT cells with and without V3 treatment.

claims.claim: Cells from Ccr5+/- mice still displayed a similar proportion of LTP after V3 treatment compared to control conditions.
claims.source: Cells from Ccr5+/- mice still displayed a similar proportion of LTP (75% V3-treated vs 62.5% control, Figure 9D) but showed significantly lower potentiation than in control conditions (127% V3 vs 208% control, Figure 9C, t(120) = 42.2, p<0.001, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro electrophysiology data comparing the proportion of cells exhibiting LTP in Ccr5+/- mice with and without V3 treatment.

claims.claim: Cells from Ccr5+/- mice showed significantly lower potentiation after V3 treatment than in control conditions.
claims.source: Cells from Ccr5+/- mice still displayed a similar proportion of LTP (75% V3-treated vs 62.5% control, Figure 9D) but showed significantly lower potentiation than in control conditions (127% V3 vs 208% control, Figure 9C, t(120) = 42.2, p<0.001, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.001) of in vitro electrophysiology data comparing LTP magnitude in Ccr5+/- cells with and without V3 treatment.

claims.claim: Cells from Ccr5-/- mice were not affected by V3 treatment in terms of LTP probability.
claims.source: In contrast, cells from mice lacking CCR5 (Ccr5-/- mice) were not affected by V3 treatment at all, with higher probability of LTP (86% V3 vs 66% control, Figure 9F) and a similar magnitude of potentiation (186% V3 vs 182% control, Figure 9E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro electrophysiology data comparing the proportion of cells exhibiting LTP in Ccr5-/- mice with and without V3 treatment.

claims.claim: Cells from Ccr5-/- mice showed a similar magnitude of potentiation with and without V3 treatment.
claims.source: In contrast, cells from mice lacking CCR5 (Ccr5-/- mice) were not affected by V3 treatment at all, with higher probability of LTP (86% V3 vs 66% control, Figure 9F) and a similar magnitude of potentiation (186% V3 vs 182% control, Figure 9E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro electrophysiology data comparing LTP magnitude in Ccr5-/- cells with and without V3 treatment.

claims.claim: V3 peptide caused LTP deficits in hippocampal slices from WT mice.
claims.source: Analyses of hippocampal slices, that had been pre-incubated 1 hr with 200 pM V3 peptide, revealed Schaffer collateral fEPSPs LTP deficits between 50 and 60 min post-TBS (theta burst stimulation) in WT (Figure 9G, t(14) = 2.53, p<0.05, Student's t-test)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.05) of in vitro electrophysiology data comparing LTP in hippocampal slices from WT mice with and without V3 treatment.

claims.claim: V3 peptide did not cause LTP deficits in hippocampal slices from Ccr5+/- mice.
claims.source: Analyses of hippocampal slices, that had been pre-incubated 1 hr with 200 pM V3 peptide, revealed Schaffer collateral fEPSPs LTP deficits between 50 and 60 min post-TBS (theta burst stimulation) in WT (Figure 9G, t(14) = 2.53, p<0.05, Student's t-test), but not from Ccr5+/- (Figure 9H, t(13) = 1.74, p=0.105, Student's t-test) and Ccr5-/- mice (Figure 9I, t(12) = 0.994, p=0.340, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.105) of in vitro electrophysiology data comparing LTP in hippocampal slices from Ccr5+/- mice with and without V3 treatment.

claims.claim: V3 peptide did not cause LTP deficits in hippocampal slices from Ccr5-/- mice.
claims.source: Analyses of hippocampal slices, that had been pre-incubated 1 hr with 200 pM V3 peptide, revealed Schaffer collateral fEPSPs LTP deficits between 50 and 60 min post-TBS (theta burst stimulation) in WT (Figure 9G, t(14) = 2.53, p<0.05, Student's t-test), but not from Ccr5+/- (Figure 9H, t(13) = 1.74, p=0.105, Student's t-test) and Ccr5-/- mice (Figure 9I, t(12) = 0.994, p=0.340, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.340) of in vitro electrophysiology data comparing LTP in hippocampal slices from Ccr5-/- mice with and without V3 treatment.

claims.claim: V3 peptide causes LTP deficits both in barrel cortex and hippocampus.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that V3 peptide causes LTP deficits both in barrel cortex and hippocampus.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined in vitro electrophysiology data from barrel cortex and hippocampus showing LTP deficits with V3 treatment.

claims.claim: V3 peptide infusion 30 min before fear conditioning caused contextual memory deficits in C57BL/6N mice.
claims.source: When injected 30 min before fear conditioning, V3 peptide caused contextual memory deficits in C57BL/6N mice (Figure 10B, t(10) = 4.04, p<0.01, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.01) of behavioral data comparing contextual fear conditioning in mice with and without V3 peptide infusion before training.

claims.claim: V3 peptide infusions following training did not affect contextual fear memory.
claims.source: In contrast, V3 peptide infusions following training did not affect contextual fear memory (Figure 10C, t(18) = 0.92, p=0.37, Student's t-test), indicating that the V3 peptide must be present during training to disrupt learning and memory.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.37) of behavioral data comparing contextual fear conditioning in mice with V3 peptide infusion immediately after training.

claims.claim: The V3 peptide must be present during training to disrupt learning and memory.
claims.source: In contrast, V3 peptide infusions following training did not affect contextual fear memory (Figure 10C, t(18) = 0.92, p=0.37, Student's t-test), indicating that the V3 peptide must be present during training to disrupt learning and memory.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the behavioral data showing that V3 peptide only causes memory deficits when present before training, not after.

claims.claim: The V3-induced memory deficit was prevented by the Ccr5+/- mutation.
claims.source: When V3 peptide was infused into the hippocampus of WT, Ccr5+/- or Ccr5-/- mice 30 min before training (Figure 10D), the V3-induced memory deficit was prevented by the Ccr5+/- or Ccr5-/- mutation [Figure 10E; Two-way ANOVA, overall (genotype × treatment) interaction: F(2,50) = 1.0; Main effect of treatment: F(1,50) = 11.10, Post hoc linear contrast: WT/Cont versus WT/V3, t(50) = 3.25 p<0.01, Bonferroni post-tests].
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-tests) of behavioral data comparing contextual fear conditioning in WT, Ccr5+/-, and Ccr5-/- mice with and without V3 peptide infusion.

claims.claim: The V3-induced memory deficit was prevented by the Ccr5-/- mutation.
claims.source: When V3 peptide was infused into the hippocampus of WT, Ccr5+/- or Ccr5-/- mice 30 min before training (Figure 10D), the V3-induced memory deficit was prevented by the Ccr5+/- or Ccr5-/- mutation [Figure 10E; Two-way ANOVA, overall (genotype × treatment) interaction: F(2,50) = 1.0; Main effect of treatment: F(1,50) = 11.10, Post hoc linear contrast: WT/Cont versus WT/V3, t(50) = 3.25 p<0.01, Bonferroni post-tests].
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-tests) of behavioral data comparing contextual fear conditioning in WT, Ccr5+/-, and Ccr5-/- mice with and without V3 peptide infusion.

claims.claim: V3 peptide caused memory deficits in shRNA-Cont mice.
claims.source: Similar to the effects in WT mice, V3 peptide caused memory deficits in shRNA-Cont mice. Importantly, these deficits were prevented by hippocampal Ccr5 knockdown [Figure 10F; Two-way ANOVA, overall (shRNA virus × treatment) interaction: F(1,34) = 0.61; Main effect of treatment: F(1,34) = 7.19; Post hoc linear contrast: shRNA-Cont/Cont versus shRNA-Cont/V3, t(34) = 2.45 p<0.05; shRNA-Cont/Cont versus shRNA-CCR5/Cont, t(34) = 2.55 p<0.05; shRNA-Cont/V3 versus shRNA-CCR5/V3, t(34) = 3.50 p<0.01, Bonferroni post-tests]
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-tests) of behavioral data comparing contextual fear conditioning in mice injected with shRNA-Cont AAV with and without V3 peptide infusion.

claims.claim: V3-induced memory deficits were prevented by hippocampal Ccr5 knockdown.
claims.source: Similar to the effects in WT mice, V3 peptide caused memory deficits in shRNA-Cont mice. Importantly, these deficits were prevented by hippocampal Ccr5 knockdown [Figure 10F; Two-way ANOVA, overall (shRNA virus × treatment) interaction: F(1,34) = 0.61; Main effect of treatment: F(1,34) = 7.19; Post hoc linear contrast: shRNA-Cont/Cont versus shRNA-Cont/V3, t(34) = 2.45 p<0.05; shRNA-Cont/Cont versus shRNA-CCR5/Cont, t(34) = 2.55 p<0.05; shRNA-Cont/V3 versus shRNA-CCR5/V3, t(34) = 3.50 p<0.01, Bonferroni post-tests], demonstrating that CCR5 is an in vivo target for the V3 peptide-dependent memory deficits.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-tests) of behavioral data comparing contextual fear conditioning in mice injected with shRNA-Cont or shRNA-CCR5 AAV with and without V3 peptide infusion.

claims.claim: CCR5 is an in vivo target for the V3 peptide-dependent memory deficits.
claims.source: Similar to the effects in WT mice, V3 peptide caused memory deficits in shRNA-Cont mice. Importantly, these deficits were prevented by hippocampal Ccr5 knockdown [Figure 10F; Two-way ANOVA, overall (shRNA virus × treatment) interaction: F(1,34) = 0.61; Main effect of treatment: F(1,34) = 7.19; Post hoc linear contrast: shRNA-Cont/Cont versus shRNA-Cont/V3, t(34) = 2.45 p<0.05; shRNA-Cont/Cont versus shRNA-CCR5/Cont, t(34) = 2.55 p<0.05; shRNA-Cont/V3 versus shRNA-CCR5/V3, t(34) = 3.50 p<0.01, Bonferroni post-tests], demonstrating that CCR5 is an in vivo target for the V3 peptide-dependent memory deficits.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the behavioral data showing that Ccr5 knockdown prevents V3-induced memory deficits.

claims.claim: V3 peptide resulted in a significant decrease in pMAPK in the dorsal hippocampal CA1 subregion at 1 hr after learning.
claims.source: Compared to controls, V3 peptide resulted in a significant decrease in pMAPK (Figure 11B, t(11) = 2.71 p<0.05, Student's t-test), but had no effect on pCREB (Figure 11C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.05) of western blot data comparing phosphorylated MAPK levels in mice with and without V3 peptide infusion.

claims.claim: V3 peptide had no effect on pCREB in the dorsal hippocampal CA1 subregion at 3 hr after learning.
claims.source: Compared to controls, V3 peptide resulted in a significant decrease in pMAPK (Figure 11B, t(11) = 2.71 p<0.05, Student's t-test), but had no effect on pCREB (Figure 11C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data comparing phosphorylated CREB levels in mice with and without V3 peptide infusion.

claims.claim: V3 peptide caused a decrease in pMAPK activation after learning in mice injected with shRNA-Cont AAV.
claims.source: A similar decrease in pMAPK was observed when the V3 peptide was infused into the hippocampus of mice injected with shRNA-Cont AAV. Importantly, this decrease in pMAPK activation after learning was ameliorated by hippocampal Ccr5 knockdown [Figure 11D; Two-way ANOVA, overall (shRNA virus × treatment) interaction: F(1,28) = 0.35; Main effect of treatment: F(1,28) = 11.8, Post hoc linear contrast: shRNA-Cont/Cont versus shRNA-Cont/V3, t(28) = 2.85 p<0.05; shRNA-Cont/V3 versus shRNA-CCR5/V3, t(28) = 2.48 p<0.05, Bonferroni post-tests].
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-tests) of western blot data comparing phosphorylated MAPK levels in mice injected with shRNA-Cont AAV with and without V3 peptide infusion.

claims.claim: The decrease in pMAPK activation after learning caused by V3 peptide was ameliorated by hippocampal Ccr5 knockdown.
claims.source: A similar decrease in pMAPK was observed when the V3 peptide was infused into the hippocampus of mice injected with shRNA-Cont AAV. Importantly, this decrease in pMAPK activation after learning was ameliorated by hippocampal Ccr5 knockdown [Figure 11D; Two-way ANOVA, overall (shRNA virus × treatment) interaction: F(1,28) = 0.35; Main effect of treatment: F(1,28) = 11.8, Post hoc linear contrast: shRNA-Cont/Cont versus shRNA-Cont/V3, t(28) = 2.85 p<0.05; shRNA-Cont/V3 versus shRNA-CCR5/V3, t(28) = 2.48 p<0.05, Bonferroni post-tests].
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-tests) of western blot data comparing phosphorylated MAPK levels in mice injected with shRNA-Cont or shRNA-CCR5 AAV with and without V3 peptide infusion.

claims.claim: Mice injected with shRNA-CCR5 AAV did not show enhanced pMAPK compared to shRNA-Cont mice.
claims.source: Interestingly, unlike the Ccr5+/- mice, that showed enhanced pMAPK activation after learning (Figure 2B), compared to shRNA-Cont mice, mice injected with shRNA-CCR5 AAV did not show enhanced pMAPK, probably because in these mice Ccr5 was knocked down in only the subset of hippocampal neurons transfected by the AAV virus.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data comparing phosphorylated MAPK levels in mice injected with shRNA-Cont and shRNA-CCR5 AAV.

claims.claim: In mice injected with shRNA-CCR5 AAV, Ccr5 was knocked down in only the subset of hippocampal neurons transfected by the AAV virus.
claims.source: Interestingly, unlike the Ccr5+/- mice, that showed enhanced pMAPK activation after learning (Figure 2B), compared to shRNA-Cont mice, mice injected with shRNA-CCR5 AAV did not show enhanced pMAPK, probably because in these mice Ccr5 was knocked down in only the subset of hippocampal neurons transfected by the AAV virus.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that shRNA-CCR5 mice did not show enhanced pMAPK like Ccr5+/- mice, and the known limitation of AAV transfection efficiency.

claims.claim: Decreasing CCR5 protects against the acute deficits caused by V3 peptide on hippocampal MAPK signaling, synaptic plasticity, and learning and memory.
claims.source: Altogether, these results indicate that decreasing CCR5 protects against the acute deficits caused by V3 peptide on hippocampal MAPK signaling, synaptic plasticity, and learning and memory, a result consistent with the idea that CCR5 activation contributes to the cognitive deficits triggered by HIV proteins.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined results from experiments showing that Ccr5 knockout or knockdown prevents V3-induced deficits in MAPK signaling, LTP, and memory.

claims.claim: CCR5 activation contributes to the cognitive deficits triggered by HIV proteins.
claims.source: Altogether, these results indicate that decreasing CCR5 protects against the acute deficits caused by V3 peptide on hippocampal MAPK signaling, synaptic plasticity, and learning and memory, a result consistent with the idea that CCR5 activation contributes to the cognitive deficits triggered by HIV proteins.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined results showing that V3 peptide causes deficits via CCR5 activation, and that decreasing CCR5 prevents these deficits.

claims.claim: CCR5 is a chemokine receptor that plays an important role in inflammatory responses.
claims.source: CCR5 is a chemokine receptor that plays an important role in inflammatory responses.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CCR5.

claims.claim: The Ccr5 knockout results in enhanced learning and memory for contextual fear conditioning.
claims.source: A learning and memory reverse genetic screen showed that the Ccr5 knockout results in enhanced learning and memory for contextual fear conditioning.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from the reverse genetic screen showing enhanced contextual fear conditioning in Ccr5 knockout mice.

claims.claim: The Ccr5 knockout did not affect anxiety, activity, social interaction, cued conditioning, and shock reactivity.
claims.source: Importantly, the Ccr5 knockout did not affect a number of behaviors that could have confounded the learning and memory findings, including anxiety, activity, social interaction, cued conditioning, and shock reactivity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from multiple behavioral assays showing no differences in these measures between Ccr5 knockout and WT mice.

claims.claim: The enhancement in learning and memory in Ccr5 knockout mice is consistent with increases in plasticity at the systems and cellular levels.
claims.source: This enhancement in learning and memory is consistent with increases in plasticity at the systems and cellular levels.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed enhancements in learning and memory and the known relationship between plasticity and learning.

claims.claim: Ccr5 knockout results in dramatically accelerated experience-dependent plasticity in the barrel cortex.
claims.source: In the barrel cortex, Ccr5 knockout results in dramatically accelerated experience-dependent plasticity: Ccr5+/- mice showed robust experience-dependent sensory plasticity at a time point (7-days after whisker removal) when WT mice show no evidence of plasticity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data showing enhanced experience-dependent plasticity in Ccr5+/- mice in the barrel cortex.

claims.claim: Temporally and spatially restricted knockdown of Ccr5, specifically in adult hippocampus or barrel cortex, resulted in enhancements in learning and memory as well as experience-dependent plasticity.
claims.source: Importantly, temporally and spatially restricted knockdown of Ccr5, specifically in adult hippocampus or barrel cortex, also resulted in enhancements in learning and memory as well as experience-dependent plasticity, demonstrating that these effects are not due to changes during development.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral and electrophysiological data from mice with viral-mediated Ccr5 knockdown in adult brain regions.

claims.claim: The effects of Ccr5 knockout on learning, memory, and plasticity are not due to changes during development.
claims.source: Importantly, temporally and spatially restricted knockdown of Ccr5, specifically in adult hippocampus or barrel cortex, also resulted in enhancements in learning and memory as well as experience-dependent plasticity, demonstrating that these effects are not due to changes during development.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that adult-specific Ccr5 knockdown produces similar effects to constitutive knockout.

claims.claim: MAPK and CREB have been implicated in learning and memory.
claims.source: MAPK and CREB have been implicated in learning and memory (Bourtchuladze et al., 1994; Roth and Sweatt, 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bourtchuladze et al., 1994; Roth and Sweatt, 2008).

claims.claim: The Ccr5 knockout did not alter MAPK or CREB signaling under baseline conditions.

results.result: Ccr5-/- and Ccr5+/- mice show enhanced contextual fear memory at 24 hours and 2 weeks after training, with normal baseline activity, shock sensitivity, and no changes in tone conditioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 provide converging evidence from multiple behavioral assays with appropriate statistical tests (t-tests, p<0.05 or p<0.01) showing enhanced contextual memory in both homozygous and heterozygous Ccr5 mutants. Control experiments demonstrate the specificity of the effect by ruling out confounds from activity, shock sensitivity, and non-specific conditioning changes.

results.result: Ccr5+/- mice demonstrate enhanced spatial learning in the Morris water maze and enhanced social recognition memory compared to WT mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 show that Ccr5+/- mice exhibit enhanced performance in two additional hippocampal-dependent memory tasks (water maze and social recognition) with appropriate statistical analyses (Two-way ANOVA, t-tests, p<0.05 or p<0.01). The use of early probe tests (2 days training) when WT mice fail to learn demonstrates the robustness of the enhancement.

results.result: The memory enhancements in Ccr5+/- mice are not confounded by changes in anxiety, locomotor activity, astrogliosis, apoptosis, or spine density.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C16 provide comprehensive control experiments ruling out alternative explanations for the memory phenotype. Multiple behavioral assays (elevated plus maze, open field) and histological analyses (GFAP, TUNEL, spine density) show no differences between genotypes, supporting the specificity of the memory enhancement.

results.result: Ccr5+/- mice show enhanced MAPK and CREB signaling at 1 and 3 hours after fear conditioning, respectively, with no baseline differences, suggesting these signaling changes are integral to memory enhancement.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 demonstrate training-induced increases in phosphorylated MAPK (1h, p<0.01) and CREB (3h, p<0.05) in Ccr5+/- mice with appropriate controls showing no baseline differences. Claim C30 appropriately infers the functional significance based on established roles of these pathways in memory, though causality is not directly tested here.

results.result: Ccr5+/- mice exhibit enhanced hippocampal LTP, suggesting CCR5 functions as a plasticity and memory suppressor.
results.evaluation: Claim C31 provides electrophysiological evidence for enhanced LTP in Ccr5+/- mice (p<0.05). Claims C32-C33 appropriately integrate the signaling, LTP, and behavioral data to conclude that CCR5 acts as a memory suppressor, though the causal chain is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Adult-specific knockdown of Ccr5 in hippocampal CA1/CA2 neurons using AAV-shRNA is sufficient to enhance contextual and spatial memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C44 demonstrate that viral-mediated Ccr5 knockdown in adult hippocampus (verified by qPCR, p<0.001) specifically in neurons (verified by immunohistochemistry) enhances both contextual fear conditioning (p<0.01) and water maze performance (p<0.001, p<0.05). This addresses developmental confounds and establishes sufficiency of adult hippocampal CCR5 reduction for memory enhancement.

results.result: CCR5 overexpression in transgenic mice causes learning and memory deficits in contextual fear conditioning and Morris water maze tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C50 show that CCR5 Tg mice with increased Ccr5 mRNA exhibit memory deficits in context pre-exposure fear conditioning (p=0.001) and water maze (p<0.001, p<0.05), with the ability to learn with extended training. This bidirectional manipulation strengthens the conclusion that CCR5 suppresses memory.

results.result: CCR5 Tg mice show decreased phospho-CREB levels at 3 hours after fear conditioning, suggesting memory deficits are due to impaired CREB-mediated memory consolidation.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 show that CCR5 Tg mice have normal baseline MAPK/CREB but decreased pCREB at 3h post-training. Claims C54-C55 appropriately link this to memory consolidation deficits based on established CREB function, though the causal mechanism is inferred rather than directly tested.

results.result: Ccr5+/- mice show accelerated experience-dependent plasticity in barrel cortex after 7 days of single whisker experience, a timepoint when WT mice show no plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 provide multiple converging measures (penetration responses, vibrissae dominance, WVDI) demonstrating enhanced barrel cortex plasticity in Ccr5+/- mice at 7 days (p<0.01, p<0.05), when WT mice show no plasticity (supported by citation C58). This extends the memory suppressor role to sensory cortex plasticity.

results.result: Ccr5+/- and Ccr5-/- mice show dramatically increased probability and magnitude of spike-timing dependent LTP in barrel cortex L2/3 neurons compared to WT mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 demonstrate that a spike-timing protocol induces LTP in 70% of Ccr5 mutant cells versus 20% in WT (p<0.001), with substantial potentiation in mutants (188% and 165%) versus no average LTP in WT. This provides cellular mechanism for enhanced cortical plasticity.

results.result: Ccr5+/- and Ccr5-/- mice exhibit lower synaptic release probability and smaller, less frequent mEPSPs in barrel cortex, potentially creating greater headroom for LTP.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 provide electrophysiological evidence for reduced release probability (p<0.01) and altered mEPSP properties (p<0.001) in Ccr5 mutants. Claim C73 appropriately infers the functional consequence (increased headroom for plasticity), consistent with similar findings in HRasG12V mice (C69), though the causal link is not directly tested.

results.result: Adult-specific viral knockdown of Ccr5 in barrel cortex neurons recapitulates the enhanced experience-dependent plasticity phenotype of Ccr5+/- mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 demonstrate that AAV-mediated Ccr5 knockdown in adult barrel cortex neurons (verified by immunohistochemistry) produces enhanced vibrissae dominance plasticity (p<0.001) similar to Ccr5+/- mice (p<0.01). This establishes that CCR5 acts directly on adult cortical neurons to suppress plasticity.

results.result: HIV gp120 V3 peptide causes LTP deficits in barrel cortex and hippocampus of WT mice, but these deficits are prevented or reduced in Ccr5+/- and Ccr5-/- mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C88 demonstrate that V3 peptide (which binds CCR5, verified by co-IP) abolishes LTP in WT cortex (p<0.001) and hippocampus (p<0.05), but has reduced or no effect in Ccr5 mutants. This provides strong evidence that CCR5 mediates V3-induced plasticity deficits, with appropriate dose-response controls.

results.result: V3 peptide infusion 30 minutes before training causes contextual memory deficits, but infusion immediately after training has no effect, indicating V3 must be present during training.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 show that V3 peptide causes memory deficits when given before training (p<0.01) but not after (p=0.37), appropriately demonstrating temporal specificity. This suggests V3/CCR5 affects encoding or early consolidation rather than late consolidation or retrieval.

results.result: V3-induced memory deficits are prevented by Ccr5+/-, Ccr5-/- mutations or hippocampal Ccr5 knockdown, demonstrating CCR5 is an in vivo target for V3-dependent memory impairment.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 provide comprehensive genetic rescue experiments showing that reducing CCR5 function (knockout or knockdown) prevents V3-induced memory deficits (Two-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests, p<0.01, p<0.05). This establishes CCR5 as the critical mediator of V3's cognitive effects.

results.result: V3 peptide decreases hippocampal pMAPK levels at 1 hour after learning, and this decrease is ameliorated by Ccr5 knockdown.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 demonstrate that V3 reduces pMAPK (p<0.05) but not pCREB after learning, and that Ccr5 knockdown prevents this pMAPK reduction (Two-way ANOVA, p<0.05). This provides a mechanistic link between V3/CCR5 activation and impaired memory consolidation signaling.

results.result: Unlike Ccr5+/- mice, shRNA-CCR5 mice do not show enhanced pMAPK after learning, likely due to incomplete knockdown in only AAV-transfected neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 appropriately note the difference between constitutive heterozygous knockout and partial viral knockdown, with a reasonable explanation based on transfection efficiency. This demonstrates awareness of experimental limitations and appropriate interpretation of negative results.

results.result: Decreasing CCR5 protects against V3-induced deficits in MAPK signaling, synaptic plasticity, and memory, suggesting CCR5 activation contributes to HIV-associated cognitive deficits.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 appropriately synthesize the V3 peptide experiments to conclude that CCR5 mediates HIV protein-induced cognitive deficits. While the inference to HIV-associated cognitive disorders is reasonable given the evidence, it remains somewhat speculative as it's based on acute peptide effects rather than chronic HIV infection models.

results.result: CCR5 functions as a plasticity and memory suppressor through MAPK/CREB signaling, and its inappropriate activation by HIV proteins contributes to cognitive deficits, while decreasing CCR5 function robustly increases plasticity and memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C140 provide an appropriate synthesis of the entire study, integrating genetic, viral, pharmacological, and overexpression data to conclude that CCR5 is a memory suppressor acting through MAPK/CREB. The evidence from bidirectional manipulations (loss and gain of function) and rescue experiments strongly supports this conclusion.

results.result: MAPK and CREB have established central roles in hippocampal learning and memory and cortical plasticity, with enhanced signaling associated with memory enhancements.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C29 appropriately cite established literature to provide context for the signaling studies. The citations appear appropriate and support the general knowledge claims about MAPK/CREB function in plasticity and memory.

results.result: Single whisker experience produces experience-dependent plasticity in barrel cortex, with 7 days being insufficient for WT mice to show potentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 cite established literature (Fox 1992, Glazewski and Fox 1996) to provide context for the barrel cortex plasticity experiments. These are appropriate background claims that establish the experimental paradigm.

results.result: Similar to HRasG12V mice, Ccr5+/- mice show lower release probability and mini-amplitudes, consistent with enhanced plasticity phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C69 and C118 appropriately compare the Ccr5 mutant phenotype to the well-characterized HRasG12V model, with proper citations. This comparison strengthens the interpretation by linking to an established plasticity enhancement model.

results.result: The HIV gp120 V3 loop peptide binds and activates CCR5, and V3-induced LTP deficits have been reported to be blocked by CXCR4 antagonists.
results.evaluation: Claims C78, C129, C131-C132 cite appropriate literature establishing V3 peptide's interaction with CCR5 and CXCR4. The citations support the rationale for using V3 peptide as a tool to activate CCR5, though the authors appropriately note that both receptors may be involved.

results.result: Previous studies have shown that HIV viral proteins cause neuronal degeneration and cognitive deficits that can be ameliorated by Ccr5 mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 cite relevant prior work (Maung et al. 2014, Tang et al. 2009) establishing the context for HIV protein effects on cognition. These citations appropriately support the rationale for investigating CCR5's role in HIV-associated cognitive deficits.

results.result: CCR5 antagonists have shown efficacy in reducing viral load in clinical studies, supporting their potential application for treating HIV-associated cognitive deficits.
results.evaluation: Claim C135 appropriately cites clinical studies showing CCR5 antagonist efficacy for viral load. However, claim C136's suggestion to use CCR5 antagonists for cognitive deficits is speculative, as the current study uses acute peptide models rather than chronic HIV infection, and clinical cognitive outcomes with CCR5 antagonists are not established.

results.result: CCR5 provides a novel target for cognitive enhancement and treatment of cognitive deficits.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C142 suggest CCR5 as a therapeutic target for cognitive enhancement and deficit treatment. While the data support CCR5's role in memory suppression, the translational implications are speculative. Safety concerns about chronic CCR5 inhibition, potential side effects, and efficacy in disease contexts are not addressed.
